candidate.title: Fake Subscription Renewal Email Scam
candidate.summary: Scammers send urgent emails impersonating well-known subscription brands like antivirus software or satellite radio, claiming your membership is expiring or auto-renewing, to steal payment details or lure you into a phone-based scam.
safetyTips: Don't click links or call phone numbers in the email; instead log into your account directly through the company's known website or app to check your actual subscription status
If you must call, use the company's verified customer service number from its official website, not one listed in the email
Keep a personal calendar of your subscriptions and auto-renewal dates so you can quickly tell when a renewal notice doesn't match reality
Never provide payment card information or online banking logins in response to an unsolicited renewal email or phone call
Report suspicious emails to the BBB Scam Tracker and the impersonated company to help warn others
candidate.howItWorks:
You receive an urgent-sounding email from what looks like a business you already have a membership or account with, stating your subscription or membership has expired or is about to auto-renew for a specific dollar amount. The email may look legitimate, including the business's logo and an invoice-style breakdown with a fake invoice number, transaction ID, and renewal date, and it often arrives suspiciously close to when a real subscription would be due. The email asks you to click a link to "update" payment information, sometimes dangling a discount for acting immediately, or it provides a customer service phone number to call to cancel the unwanted "renewal." Victims who click the link and enter card details end up on a fake site that steals their financial information and may even charge their card, while victims who call the provided number are connected to a scammer posing as support staff who pressures them to log into online banking or move money, using fake on-screen banking confirmations to appear convincing.</howItWorks>
<redFlags>["Urgent email claiming a subscription or membership is expiring or auto-renewing for a specific amount", "A customer service or 'cancellation' phone number embedded directly in the email rather than on the company's real website", "Request to click a link and enter payment card details to 'renew' or 'cancel' a subscription you don't recall signing up for", "Email arrives suspiciously close to a real subscription renewal date, making it seem more credible", "Pressure to act within 24 hours or lose a discount or avoid an unwanted charge"]
redFlags: Urgent email claiming a subscription or membership is expiring or auto-renewing for a specific amount
A customer service or 'cancellation' phone number embedded directly in the email rather than on the company's real website
Request to click a link and enter payment card details to 'renew' or 'cancel' a subscription you don't recall signing up for
Email arrives suspiciously close to a real subscription renewal date, making it seem more credible
Pressure to act within 24 hours or lose a discount or avoid an unwanted charge
realExamples: A consumer reported receiving an email claiming their Sirius XM account had expired a day after their normal renewal date, directing them to a site asking them to 'insert' credit card information.

A consumer received an email styled like an invoice with a transaction ID and renewal date, offering a number to call within 24 hours to cancel a subscription they never had; the number connected to someone who insisted the cancellation needed to proceed.

An Ohio consumer reported an email posing as Norton Antivirus support asking for personal information to renew a nonexistent subscription, with the scammer walking them through a fake pending bank deposit screen to appear credible.

triage.reasoning: This is a subscription-themed instance of generic email phishing (fake urgent renewal notice with a link to steal payment info), which is already covered by the existing 'Phishing Email Scam' entry; the specific lure (subscription/membership renewal) is a variant rather than a structurally new scam mechanism. The source is a BBB consumer alert, not a government regulator or major news outlet, so credibility is classified as 'other'.
